02 Antipsychotics · class card

Tardive dyskinesia agents

Vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) inhibitors · valbenazine · deutetrabenazine · tetrabenazine

Key point
  • Valbenazine and deutetrabenazine inhibit vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) less dopamine stored for release the drugs for tardive dyskinesia
  • Tetrabenazine and reserpine deplete dopamine the same way, for Huntington chorea; tetrabenazine also treats Tourette tics
  • In Huntington disease they can deepen depression and suicidality, a boxed warning on all three labels
Drugs

Valbenazine Ingrezza: tardive dyskinesia and Huntington chorea

Deutetrabenazine Austedo: tardive dyskinesia and Huntington chorea; better tolerated than tetrabenazine Label dosingLabel: stop tetrabenazine and start deutetrabenazine the next day.

Tetrabenazine Xenazine: Huntington chorea on its label; the board example for tics Tetrabenazine and tardive dyskinesiaOn a board card, reserpine and tetrabenazine may also treat tardive dyskinesia; the labeled drugs are valbenazine and deutetrabenazine.

Mechanism

VMAT2 carries monoamines from the cytoplasm into synaptic vesicles for storage and release

Reversible VMAT2 block dopamine, serotonin and norepinephrine stores deplete less dopamine on supersensitive dopamine receptors fewer dyskinetic movements MechanismThe labels call the mechanism in tardive dyskinesia unclear; VMAT2 inhibition is the accepted account.

Depleting, not blocking no tardive dyskinesia or metabolic syndrome from these drugs

Reserpine irreversible VMAT2 block lasting days

Uses

Tardive dyskinesia, moderate to severe: valbenazine or deutetrabenazine

Huntington chorea: a VMAT2 inhibitor is typically first line

Tourette tics that still impair: tetrabenazine as the dopamine-depleting option

Adverse effects

Somnolence and sedation, the most common; no driving until the effect is known

Depression and suicidality in Huntington disease (boxed warning)

Parkinsonism and akathisia: lower the dose or stop

QT prolongation: avoid with congenital long QT syndrome or QT-related arrhythmias

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: stop the drug

Depression and suicidalityHuntington disease already carries high rates of depression and suicide; monoamine depletion can worsen both, the boxed warning on valbenazine, deutetrabenazine and tetrabenazine

Tetrabenazine and deutetrabenazine labels rule them out with active suicidality or untreated depression

If Huntington chorea comes with untreated depression or suicidal thoughts, choose an antipsychotic for the chorea, not a VMAT2 inhibitor.

Practice
  1. 61-year-old man with schizophrenia on fluphenazine for 12 years slow tongue writhing, lip pursing and facial grimacing for 6 months his psychiatrist keeps the antipsychotic and adds valbenazine no tremor · no rigidity · mood stable → Depletes dopamine from presynaptic vesicles → valbenazine reversibly inhibits vesicular monoamine transporter 2, so less dopamine is stored and released onto the supersensitive receptors behind tardive dyskinesia; receptor blockade by fluphenazine caused the movements, and muscarinic blockade can worsen them
  2. 46-year-old woman with genetically confirmed Huntington disease chorea now spills her drinks and wakes her husband low mood, anhedonia and passive thoughts of death for 2 months, untreated no plan or intent · no prior attempt → Tetrabenazine → depleting monoamines can worsen depression and suicidality in Huntington disease, and its label rules it out with untreated depression or active suicidality; an antipsychotic is the alternative first line for chorea with depression, and sertraline may help the mood
  3. 52-year-old man with Huntington disease and a good mood chorea makes him drop utensils and spill food at meals tetrabenazine is started and the movements lessen over weeks no depression · no parkinsonism → Reserpine → tetrabenazine and reserpine both inhibit vesicular monoamine transporter 2, so less dopamine is packaged and released; reserpine binds irreversibly and its effect lasts days; haloperidol blocks dopamine receptors and benztropine blocks muscarinic receptors
